title: Turn your identity governance investment into business value
summary: Identity governance is more than a compliance requirement. Discover how OpenText NetIQ Identity Governance helps organizations reduce access risk, simplify access reviews, improve decision-making, and transform identity governance into a driver of operational efficiency and business value.
body_markdown:
After weeks or months of evaluation, you’ve chosen an[identity governance solution](https://www.opentext.com/what-is/identity-governance-administration) to help reduce inappropriate access, simplify reviews, strengthen audit evidence, and replace manual processes. Now that the purchase is complete, the next challenge is turning those capabilities into results.


Maybe you’ve connected your first applications and completed an access review. Or maybe your program already covers much of the enterprise. Either way, the value you get depends on how effectively the business participates: how access decisions are made, how job changes translate into access changes, and what you choose to improve next.


Organizations get more business value from identity governance when reviewers have clear context, business rules reflect job changes, and approved access removals are verified. The platform provides capabilities. Your governance program puts them to work.


# Make the investment count


You’ve probably seen it happen. A company buys new software, works hard to get it running, and then moves on to the next priority. Six months later, someone asks, “Are we getting what we expected?” The answer isn’t always clear. Sometimes, it’s an obvious “no.” Software can be up and running without changing the way people make decisions, so the real test comes after rollout.


Think about an early identity governance review. A manager approves an employee’s access because the permission names make no sense, so the manager assumes it’s all needed. Or the manager flags access for removal, but no one follows through. The review is complete, yet the risk remains.[OpenText™ NetIQ™ Identity Governance](https://www.opentext.com/products/identity-governance) can provide clear, useful identity and access information, but getting that value takes some setup and ongoing attention. A technically complete review doesn’t help much if the reviewer lacks context or the resulting actions never happen.


That’s why it helps to revisit what you wanted to accomplish. If better access decisions were a priority, you need to give managers useful context, encourage them to act on it, and make sure their decisions lead to real changes.


# Give reviewers context for better decisions


Imagine you’re a manager opening an[access review](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/user_guide_review_definitions) . You see a list of employees and permissions with names like “FIN_AP_03.” Should Sarah have that access? You know what Sarah does, but that code tells you nothing about what she can do in the application. You’re left guessing—or asking someone to explain it.


Now imagine that permission is described as “Approve supplier payments up to $25,000.” You can make an informed decision. Sarah handles supplier inquiries, but approving payments isn’t part of her job. You flag that access for removal.


That’s where a well-implemented identity governance solution makes a difference.[Collectors](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/user_guide_b1e56ljh) bring together identity, account, and permission data from connected applications. The[governance catalog](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/user_guide_b19ktrko) helps organize it. But someone who knows the application still needs to describe what the permissions mean and identify the right reviewers. That’s how technical permissions become information a manager can use, rather than another set of codes to interpret.


You know it’s working when reviewers don’t have to decipher permissions or figure out whom to ask. Application owners can explain what each permission allows and why it matters to the business. Compliance and audit teams can help clarify what evidence the organization needs to retain.


Pay attention to the questions reviewers ask, too. If several managers need help understanding the same permission, improve its description. If reviews keep being forwarded, check whether they’re going to the right people. Each adjustment makes the next review easier and the decisions more useful.


# Put business rules to work


Now Sarah is moving from finance to operations, and her new manager wants her ready to work on Monday. Everyone is focused on giving her the access she needs. But who’s checking what she should leave behind?


Without a clear process, Sarah could carry her old finance access into her new job. It might stay there until the next scheduled review, even though she no longer needs it.


This is where business rules can help.[Business roles](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/user_guide_create_br) can define the access someone in Sarah’s new position typically needs. Technical roles can group related permissions so they’re easier to manage. When updated employee data reaches the governance catalog,[data policies](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/user_guide_t4axgs4oci74) can help identify changes that need attention and trigger a focused review.


People still need to make the judgment calls. Should Sarah keep some finance access while she finishes a handoff? Who approves that exception, and when should it end? Once those decisions are made, configured provisioning and fulfillment processes can carry out the access changes.


Start with a single transfer scenario like Sarah’s. Bring the right managers and application owners together, agree on what should happen, and verify that it does. When that process works, you have a practical model to build on.


# Prove the value and build on progress


Sarah’s manager has decided to remove her old finance access. That’s the right call. But could Sarah still sign in and approve a payment a week later? If the organization hasn’t followed through and verified the removal, that access might still be active.


That’s why approving removal isn’t the same as completing it.[Fulfillment](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/user_guide_monitor_fulfillment) carries the decision into the relevant application, and a subsequent collection can confirm whether the access is gone. If it’s still there, you have a specific problem to investigate. Was a task missed? Did an automated change fail? Is it unclear who should act?


The same principle applies across your governance program.[Insights and reporting](https://docs.microfocus.com/doc/2335/25.4/techref_t4mbayvcz9nq) can show where you’re making progress and where work gets stuck. Are managers spending less time deciphering permissions? How long does it take to confirm that unwanted access is removed? Which applications still need governance coverage? Look for patterns, too: which approvals get delayed, which removals stall, and where reviewers repeatedly ask for clarification.


Use those answers to decide what to improve next. Maybe reviewers need clearer descriptions. Maybe access removals need more reliable follow-through. Choose a change that addresses a real problem, then check whether it helps. For more practical ideas, read Getting the most out of OpenText NetIQ Identity Governance. The guide offers ways to put the capabilities you’ve invested in to work and deliver results the business can see. The priorities are straightforward: make permissions understandable, apply business rules to access changes, and verify fulfillment.
